text: The emphasis on learning from the ingroup. <break time="0.8s" /> Takes little account of individuals. <break time="0.8s" /> Amazingly. <break time="0.8s" /> While we may dislike some of the people in our ingroup. <break time="0.8s" /> We still copy them. <break time="0.8s" /> Wilks, Kirby, and Nielsen studied copying behavior. <break time="0.8s" /> In the context of observing how to open a puzzle box. <break time="0.8s" /> Ingroups and outgroups were distinguished in a minimal way. <break time="0.8s" /> Using simple color coding of wristbands. <break time="0.8s" /> The children did not simply like all members of their ingroup. <break time="0.8s" /> They disliked those who behaved in an antisocial fashion. <break time="0.8s" /> Indeed. <break time="0.8s" /> They liked these antisocial ingroup members less. <break time="0.8s" /> Than the prosocial members of an outgroup. <break time="0.8s" /> Still. <break time="0.8s" /> Their dislike did not affect. <break time="0.8s" /> Their tendency to copy ingroup behavior more closely than outgroup behavior. <break time="0.8s" /> This overimitation reveals. <break time="0.8s" /> That we are not copying. <break time="0.8s" /> In order to learn how to open a box most efficiently. <break time="0.8s" /> We want to learn how to do it in the proper way. <break time="0.8s" /> , in other words. <break time="0.8s" /> Conforming to the rules and conventions of the ingroup. <break time="0.8s" /> This will be appropriately demonstrated. <break time="0.8s" /> Even by antisocial ingroup members.
